title: The daemon gets its first durable recurring schedule, restart-safe and never doubled
description:
SPIDR grandchild A of task-6ec875f4dd5f4f2ab97e46f71bf57b2b (architect-aa54e231, 2026-09-05), split because the parent needed the daemon's FIRST recurring loop plus a probe, a bounded ring, a derived state and an incident - five pieces over twelve-plus files. This row is the dependency-free LEAF and it is pure infrastructure. Grandchild B consumes it.

THE DAEMON HAS NO RECURRING LOOP AT ALL. Measured at HEAD (branch moe/work-2026-09-04): `grep -rn "setInterval" apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts` excluding tests returns ZERO, and daemon-main.ts has no periodic tick. Everything the daemon does today is request-driven or spawn-driven. So this row is not "add a timer to the existing scheduler" - it is the first scheduled work in the process, and that is exactly why the parent's DoD 3 hazard exists.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: a durable recurring schedule. Registered targets with a per-target interval, persisted so a restart resumes them, and an IDEMPOTENT registration so a restart cannot end up running the same target twice.

THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE IS THE SUBJECT. A restart that re-registers an already-scheduled target doubles the rate SILENTLY - the symptom is a durable store filling twice as fast, never an error, and nobody looks until the store is large. Assert the RATE across a restart, not merely that work resumed. A test that only checks "it is still scheduled" passes for a doubled schedule.

BUILD IT INJECTABLE. Take the clock and the timer as ports the way `verifier-process-runner.ts` takes `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs` and `killProcessGroup` (options at :45-56) - a scheduler tested against a real wall clock is slow and flaky, and this repo already has a spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests (~10 s stalls). Every arm here must run on a fake clock in milliseconds.

STOP CLEANLY. Timers keep a node process alive; a schedule with no shutdown path makes the daemon unkillable and makes every test that starts one leak a handle. Copy `verifier-process-runner.ts`'s discipline: one cleanup, called on every exit path, idempotent (:107-118).

NOT IN SCOPE: the health probe itself, the probe ring, UP/DEGRADED/DOWN, and the incident - all grandchild B. No UI.

VERIFY: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`.
definitionOfDone: A target registered with an interval runs on that interval, asserted on an INJECTED clock and timer rather than a real one - no arm in this row may depend on wall-clock time, because the measured spawn-latency cliff on this host reds timing-sensitive tests for unrelated reasons.

REGISTRATION IS IDEMPOTENT: registering the same target twice leaves ONE schedule, asserted by counting executions over a fixed window rather than by inspecting a registry. A registry-count assertion passes for a design that stores one entry and arms two timers.

SURVIVES A RESTART WITH NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE: rebuild the scheduler from durable records and assert the post-restart execution RATE equals the pre-restart rate over the same window. Asserting that work merely resumed is what lets a silently doubled schedule ship - and its only symptom is a store filling twice as fast.

EVERY TIMER IS RELEASED ON SHUTDOWN, asserted by the process being able to exit (or by an explicit handle count), not by a flag. A leaked interval keeps node alive and makes any test that starts a schedule leak into its neighbours.
The per-target interval is durable and a target with no interval takes a stated default; assert the default is applied rather than the target being skipped.
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`.
taskRails: NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE, AND ASSERT THE RATE. 'It resumed after restart' is the assertion that lets a doubled schedule through; only counting executions over a window catches it.
INJECTED CLOCK AND TIMER ONLY. No arm may wait on real time: this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests for reasons unrelated to the code.
ONE CLEANUP, ON EVERY EXIT PATH, IDEMPOTENT - copy verifier-process-runner.ts:107-118. A leaked interval keeps the process alive and contaminates neighbouring tests.
THIS IS THE DAEMON'S FIRST SCHEDULED WORK. Keep it generic and free of health-probe vocabulary: grandchild B is its first consumer, not its owner.
NO PROBE, NO RING, NO INCIDENT, NO UI - grandchild B and the parent's children 2 and 3.

implementationPlan.description: MEASURE AT CLAIM — NO EDITS. (a) Re-run `git grep -n "setInterval" -- apps/daemon/src` excluding `*.test.ts`. At plan time this returns ZERO production hits, which is this row's whole premise. If a recurring loop has appeared since, STOP and report: someone else built the daemon's first scheduler and this row would be a silent duplicate — `git log -- <that file>` names the owner. (b) Re-confirm the composition facts this plan rests on, because they are what parked the row once already: `createStoreDependencies` at daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:158 with the store bound LEXICALLY at :165 and NOT returned on the provider; the provider's existing SYNC `close()` at :549; `fromEnv()`'s module-level `envProvider` singleton at daemon-store-dependencies.ts:59-62; `DaemonDependencyProvider` at daemon-entry.ts:68-72 with its optional `provideV2?()` precedent; the shutdown at daemon-entry.ts:328-335; and daemon-main.ts:201/:205/:228-232. (c) CONFIRM THE FACT THIS PLAN TURNS ON: the daemon never calls `provider.close()` — `git grep -n "provider.close\|\.close()" -- apps/daemon/src` and check the daemon's chain reaches only the LISTENER's close. If that has changed, say so, because it moves where the release belongs. (d) Read the shapes to copy: verifier-process-runner.ts:45-56 and :107-118 for injected ports and one idempotent cleanup; environment-store.ts:91-115 for the commit shape; environment-projection.ts:80-87 with environment-fold.ts:12-16 for the fold and its drop policy. (e) Record the global-rail-3 baseline: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` and `pnpm typecheck`, saving the failing-file rosters for attribution in step 7.

RED TESTS FIRST, ALL ON A FAKE CLOCK, in the new module's name-matched sibling. Rail 2 is absolute: no arm may wait on wall-clock time — this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff (~10s stalls) that reds timing-sensitive tests for unrelated reasons, making failures unattributable. Inject BOTH the clock and the timer; the test drives time forward explicitly and counts executions; nothing sleeps. Write these and watch them fail: (1) INTERVAL HONOURED (DoD 1) — a target at interval N executes once per N of injected time; advance a known window and assert the EXACT execution count, not "at least once". (2) REGISTRATION IDEMPOTENT (DoD 2) — register the SAME target twice, advance a fixed window, assert the count equals the single-registration count. Assert by COUNTING EXECUTIONS, never by inspecting a registry: a design that stores one entry while arming two timers passes a registry assertion and IS the bug. (3) RESTART DOES NOT DOUBLE (DoD 3) — run a window and record the rate; rebuild the scheduler from its durable records the way a restart would; run the SAME window and assert the second rate EQUALS the first. (4) DEFAULT INTERVAL APPLIES (DoD 5) — a target registered with no interval EXECUTES at the stated default; assert it runs, not that it was skipped, since a silently skipped target looks identical to nothing registered. (5) SHUTDOWN RELEASES (DoD 4) — after release, advancing the clock produces NO further executions, AND the injected timer reports ZERO armed handles (DoD 4 explicitly accepts an explicit handle count; a boolean flag proves only that the code believed it released). A second release is harmless. Assert against the production surface; never a helper that re-derives tick counts.

THE SCHEDULER CORE — a new focused module at apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/durable-schedule.ts plus its one-line `.js` bridge (copy environment-store.js's shape). The test written in step 2 MUST be named `durable-schedule.test.ts` to match, or runtime-entrypoint.test.ts classifies the module TEST tier and reports the bridge as `unexpected`. KEEP IT GENERIC (rail 4): this is the daemon's first scheduled work and grandchild B is its FIRST CONSUMER, not its owner — no `probe`, no `health`, no `environment` vocabulary. A target is an id, an interval and a callback. Ports, all injectable, following verifier-process-runner.ts:45-56: `now(): number`, the timer pair (set/clear), and the store for step 4's durable half. FOUR POLICIES, DECIDED HERE rather than left open, because each is a seam the double-schedule can return through — implement them and state each in the step note: (1) IDEMPOTENCE — re-registering a target id already armed at the SAME interval is a NO-OP; if the interval DIFFERS, clean-replace (clear, then arm exactly one). Pure no-op would silently ignore an interval change; pure replace would re-phase the timer on every restart pass. Guard it in ONE place: if the in-memory arm and the durable write can disagree about whether a target is already scheduled, the double-schedule returns by that seam. (2) OVERLAP — if a callback is still running when its next tick arrives, SKIP rather than stack; a 90s callback on a 60s interval would otherwise accumulate concurrent runs and fill the store faster than its stated rate, the same symptom as a doubled schedule from a different cause. (3) A THROWING TARGET is contained and the next tick still fires — a probe that throws once must not silently stop all scheduling. (4) ONE IDEMPOTENT `release()` clearing every armed timer, in the shape of verifier-process-runner.ts:107-118: harmless twice, and does not throw when called mid-execution. Keep the module under 250 lines.

THE DURABLE HALF — persistence and the restart rebuild, in the same module. Persist each registered target (id, interval, and whatever a consumer needs to reconstruct its binding) in the EVENT STORE using the environment-store.ts:91-115 commit shape named in step 1 — there is no settings directory in the daemon, so the event store is the durable home. Fold on read for the current target set the way environment-projection.ts:80-87 does: later events win, and a malformed record DROPS the target rather than being ignored, matching environment-fold.ts:12-16's reasoning — silently resurrecting a stale target is the more dangerous reading, because a dropped target is visibly absent while a resurrected one runs at an interval nobody chose. THE REBUILD IS WHERE THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE HAPPENS: on start the scheduler reads its durable targets and arms them, and the hazard is a start path that arms from durable records WHILE a caller also re-registers the same targets — each individually correct, together they double the rate. Registration must be idempotent ACROSS the rebuild, not merely within one process: the durable record is the identity, so re-registering a target the rebuild already armed is a no-op under the step-3 policy. Step 2's arm 3 is what proves it. A CALLBACK CANNOT BE PERSISTED: a rebuilt target reacquires its behaviour through a consumer-supplied resolver keyed by target id, and a target the resolver cannot resolve is DROPPED with a visible refusal — never an armed timer with no work attached, which would burn an interval forever doing nothing.

COMPOSITION — THE STEP THAT PARKED THIS ROW; the old version named daemon-main.ts alone and was unsatisfiable. BUILD IT WHERE THE STORE IS A FACT: inside `createStoreDependencies` (daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:158), over the LEXICAL `store` bound at :165. Do NOT call `acquireFoundationStore` again — daemon-store-acquisition.ts:28 opens a SECOND handle, which would give the scheduler a different store from the rest of the daemon. That file is 580 lines, already past the split threshold: add only the construction call and the release line, and do not refactor it. RELEASE IN TWO PLACES, ONE FUNCTION. (a) The provider's existing `close()` at :549 also calls `release()`. Keep that close SYNC — `clearInterval` is synchronous, and the signature has six call sites (mcp-main.ts:158, agent-wrapper-main.ts:366, four fixtures) that must not be widened. (b) daemon-entry.ts's shutdown at :328-335 releases too, because **the daemon process never calls `provider.close()`** — its chain is daemon-main.ts:205 `await started.shutdown()` -> daemon-entry.ts:333 `await started.close()`, the LISTENER's close, with everything else riding on `process.exit(0)` at daemon-main.ts:229. Releasing only at (a) leaves the shipped daemon's timers armed while a provider-level test passes. EXPOSE IT as an OPTIONAL member on `DaemonDependencyProvider` (daemon-entry.ts:68-72), following the `provideV2?()` precedent for a non-read optional member — NOT on `OptionalDaemonPortProvider`, whose 28 members are all READ ports handed to the listener. Then forward it on the frozen default provider in daemon-store-dependencies.ts:64 the way every other member forwards through `fromEnv()`. THREE THINGS NOT TO DO: do not add a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler (daemon-main.ts:228-232 already registers `process.once` for both; a second would race it and could exit before the release runs); do not make the daemon call `provider.close()` as a shortcut (`fromEnv()` memoises a module-level singleton, so that closes the SHARED store process-wide — a real latent bug, but a different row: note it, do not take it); and do not treat `unref()` as the release, since an unref'd timer still FIRES while the process lives — state whether you used it and why it is not a substitute.

THE PROVIDER-KEY MIRROR — expected red, fixed honestly. daemon-store-dependencies.test.ts:727 computes `providerKeys: Object.keys(provider).sort()` and :781 asserts an EXACT roster inside a `toEqual`. Adding the scheduler member to the frozen default provider WILL red that arm: that is the exact-arity mirror doing its job, not a defect, and it is the proof that the member actually reached the SHIPPED provider rather than only a test double — which is precisely what this row was parked for failing to do. TAKE THE NEW ROSTER FROM THE PRINTED EXPECTED-VS-RECEIVED of the failing run, never by hand-writing what you think it should be. Note that this arm spawns a real child under `--experimental-strip-types` with a 180s timeout, so run it TARGETED before any full-suite leg. While you are here, confirm the arm still asserts VALUES rather than typeofs (its own comment at :735-737 says why: a binding that resolved to the wrong module, a registry that lost an entry, or a replay that ran an effect twice all have to show up here rather than pass as "it imported"). Do not weaken it to accommodate the new key.

DRILLS, THEN GATES. THREE DRILLS, each aimed at an arm that would otherwise be vacuous. (1) THE SUBJECT OF THE ROW: make the restart rebuild arm targets WITHOUT the idempotence guard; step 2's arm 3 MUST go red ON THE RATE COMPARISON. If it stays green, that arm is asserting work resumed rather than comparing rates — rewrite it before accepting, because that is exactly the assertion that lets a doubled schedule ship. (2) IDEMPOTENCE: register the same target twice with the guard removed; arm 2 must go red on the execution COUNT. If your arm inspects a registry it will stay green, which is the point of the drill. (3) THE RELEASE: remove the release from daemon-entry's shutdown; arm 5 must go red on executions-after-shutdown and on the armed-handle count, NOT on a flag. RESTORE PROOF (global rail 13): `git status --porcelain` the exact mutated paths FIRST, and say which proof applies to which — MIXED here: the three daemon files are TRACKED and take an empty `git diff -- <path>` run in a call SEPARATE from the restore; your new module, its bridge and its test are UNTRACKED and `git diff` is BLIND to them, so back each up out of tree (%TEMP%, suffixed with your worker id) and prove restoration by SHA256 equality. THEN THE GATES, each STANDALONE and FOREGROUND — no pipe, no `;` chain, no `&&` (a piped run reports tail's exit code; a chain reports only the last command's): `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, then `pnpm typecheck`. READ THE OUTPUT, NOT THE EXIT CODE: a missed `--filter` exits 0, and "No test files found"/"0 passed" are also exit 0 — the discriminator is `Test Files N passed` with N nonzero; quote it for both. A bare `pnpm test` covers no `apps/**` and is not evidence. The daemon suite is slow (~22 min) and flaky here (back-to-back baselines gave `17 failed | 416 passed` then `10 failed | 423 passed`, dominated by 30000ms timeouts), so attribute red BY PATH against step 1's saved rosters, never by whole-suite delta. WATCH FOR NEW TIMEOUTS IN UNRELATED FILES: that is the signature of a leaked interval from this row contaminating its neighbours, and it is the one red here you should treat as YOURS even though the failing file is not.

ADVERSARIAL SELF-REVIEW, THEN COMPLETE. Read the diff as an attacker: Is the scheduler reachable from the SHIPPED provider, or only through a test injection — i.e. would `node ./src/daemon-main.ts` actually arm it? (The provider-key mirror going red in step 6 and then green is your evidence; if it never red, the member did not reach the real provider and the row has repeated the mistake it was parked for.) Was a second store handle opened anywhere? Is the release genuinely ONE function called from both the provider close and daemon-entry's shutdown, idempotent, and safe mid-execution? Can a target registered twice at DIFFERENT intervals leave two armed timers? Does a callback that throws on its FIRST tick still leave the target scheduled? Does an unresolvable target after restart get dropped visibly rather than armed with no work? Did the provider's `close()` stay synchronous? THE COMPLETION RECORD must state: that this is the daemon's first recurring loop, with the grep proving it; the idempotence decision (no-op at same interval, clean-replace at a different one) and the ONE place it is guarded; the overlap policy and the throwing-target policy; how a rebuilt target reacquires its callback and what happens when it cannot; whether `unref` was used and why it is not the release; that the daemon does NOT call `provider.close()` and therefore why the release is wired in two places; the latent bug found and deliberately NOT taken (the daemon never closing its store provider, whose `fromEnv()` singleton makes that a process-wide change); and the three drill outcomes with their restore proofs. Name `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` as the complete_task verification command. Report every path created or modified in complete_step.modifiedFiles.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
RE-PLAN of my own row (I filed and first planned it). worker-7bdbffac parked it correctly: old step 5 said "the only edit to an existing file in this row" and named daemon-main.ts alone, while composing a durable scheduler needs the STORE, which daemon-main.ts cannot reach. Their analysis is confirmed in full — I re-measured every claim. Steps 1-4 and the drills survive; step 5 is replaced and the file roster widened from 1 to 4 existing files.

WHERE THE SCHEDULER IS BUILT. `createStoreDependencies` (daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:158) is the ONLY place the store is a fact: `const { foundation, store } = acquireFoundationStore(...)` at :165 is LEXICAL and never returned on the provider. Re-calling `acquireFoundationStore` opens a SECOND handle (daemon-store-acquisition.ts:28), which would give the scheduler a different store from the rest of the daemon — so construction must happen inside that function, over that binding.

HOW IT REACHES daemon-entry — THREE SEAMS EVALUATED. (a) `MainOptions` hook: REJECTED, and this is what parked the row. The shipped CLI's call at daemon-main.ts:221-233 passes only `operatorInput` and `onStarted`, so a MainOptions hook wires tests and never production — a test-injected hook substituted for real composition. (b) `OptionalDaemonPortProvider` (daemon-entry-port-resolution.ts:36, resolved shape at :118-146): WORKS but is the wrong home — all 28 members there are READ ports handed to the listener, and it costs a 486-line file plus its roster tests. (c) CHOSEN: an optional member on `DaemonDependencyProvider` itself (daemon-entry.ts:68-72), where `provideV2?()` already sets the precedent for a non-read optional member. daemon-entry reads it directly in the shutdown it already owns. Narrowest correct seam; keeps a lifecycle out of the read-port roster.

WHERE THE RELEASE HANGS — AND THE FACT THAT DECIDES IT. **The daemon process NEVER calls `provider.close()`.** Measured: `provider.close()` is called from mcp-main.ts:158, agent-wrapper-main.ts:366 and four fixtures, but the daemon's chain is daemon-main.ts:205 `await started.shutdown()` -> daemon-entry.ts:333 `await started.close()`, which closes the LISTENER; teardown otherwise rides on `process.exit(0)` in the SIGINT/SIGTERM handler at :229. So hanging the release ONLY on `provider.close()` would satisfy nothing in the shipped daemon — the exact class of mistake that parked this row. The release therefore goes in BOTH places, as ONE idempotent function: daemon-entry's shutdown (the daemon path) and the provider's existing `close()` (the wrapper and MCP paths, which do call it). Calling it twice must be harmless, which the row already requires.

WHY NOT MAKE THE DAEMON CALL provider.close() INSTEAD: it looks like the tidier fix and it is a trap. `fromEnv()` (daemon-store-dependencies.ts:59-62) memoises the provider in a module-level `envProvider` singleton, so `close()` would shut the SHARED store for the whole process. That is a much larger blast radius than this row, and a latent-bug fix that belongs to its own row — note it, do not take it.

DESIGN QUESTIONS SETTLED HERE rather than left to the worker, since each one is where the double-schedule can return: idempotence is NO-OP when the same target id is already armed at the SAME interval, and a CLEAN REPLACE (clear then arm exactly one) when the interval differs — pure no-op would silently ignore an interval change, pure replace re-phases the timer on every restart pass. Overlap: SKIP, never stack. A throwing target: contain and keep scheduling. Rebuilt callbacks: a consumer-supplied resolver keyed by target id, and an unresolvable target is DROPPED visibly, never armed with no work.
